justification: Design/UX round 1 for /csharp-dotnet/linq-deferred-execution/, a brand-new article. Verified with `node tools/verify-page.mjs --drafts /csharp-dotnet/linq-deferred-execution/` (real Lighthouse run, PowerShell, nothing else running concurrently): Lighthouse 97/100/100/100, 0 console errors, 0 console warnings, 0 broken links (7 external Microsoft Learn URLs all resolved, 27 internal links fine), mobileOverflowPx: 0. The only reported failure is the expected `placeholder text: NEEDS_MARKUS` (byline/author-bio/legal-name markers), which is accepted per docs/WRITER_GUIDE.md and docs/ARTICLE_GAUNTLET.md until the owner supplies real values. Compared against the two Microsoft Learn pages this article itself cites as primary sources, which are also the top organic results for 'LINQ deferred execution': 'Deferred execution and lazy evaluation' (fetched directly this round: 341 words, plain prose, a single bullet list contrasting lazy/eager evaluation, no diagrams, no runnable code shown inline, no measured output, no dark-mode-aware illustration) and 'Introduction to LINQ Queries', similarly text-only. This article (2427 words, 22 verified code/output blocks, 1 custom diagram) is far deeper: it demonstrates the SLA-miscount bug with real counted side effects, traces `yield return` suspend/resume with two interleaved Console trails, rebuilds `Where`/`Select` from scratch and then runs the custom and real operators side by side with matching interleaving, measures actual re-enumeration cost in milliseconds on stated hardware, and inspects a live `Expression` tree to show IQueryable's plan-vs-code distinction — none of which either Microsoft Learn page attempts. No competing tutorial-style page (TutorialsTeacher/C-SharpCorner-style) that ranks for this query offers a hand-drawn theme-aware pipeline diagram, an interleaved mine/real trace comparison, or measured timing data either, which is the norm for this content type across the web. Read every desktop-light part (01-11) and every mobile-dark part (01-17) in full; spot-checked desktop-dark fold + parts 06-07 (diagram + trace-comparison output) and mobile-light fold + parts 07-08 (diagram + trace-comparison output). The pull-based-pipeline diagram (viewBox 360x440, portrait, 4 stacked boxes with MoveNext()/one-item arrows and an annotation block underneath) renders legibly and correctly themed in all four desktop/mobile x light/dark combinations: no faded edge (it never needs to scroll, matching the writer's phone-checked claim), text readable at the 12-14 viewBox-unit sizes used, dark-mode strokes and fills have correct contrast against the dark background. All code blocks and output panels fit the ~40-column mobile window with room to spare, including the two panels flagged for special attention: the interleaved 'mine:'/'real:' trace comparison output (mobile-dark part08, mobile-light part08) tops out at about 24 visible characters per line ('  real: projecting #2') with zero clipping, and the re-enumeration timing panel ('first: 17984 primes, [...] ms', mobile-dark part10) also fits fully with the `[...]` wildcard correctly used per docs/WRITER_GUIDE.md's rule that timing digits vary. Long C# declaration lines that do run past column 40 (e.g. 'IEnumerable<Ticket> urgent = tickets.Where(t =>') are consistently the boilerplate half of a statement whose lambda body and operative logic sit on the following, fully-visible lines -- exactly the exception the phone-width rule allows. Exercise solutions are correctly collapsed behind 'Show solution' in every screenshot checked, and the predict-the-output exercise (Exercise 1) does not leak its output panel above the collapsed solution, matching the binding editorial-brief rule. Heading hierarchy is clean: exactly one h1, all seven body sections are h2 with no h3 (so 'On this page' renders as a single flat, non-nested list, which is valid per the writer guide's h2/h3-only TOC rule), and headings are specific to content rather than boilerplate Introduction/Conclusion. Reading rhythm varies well: buggy-code+output -> prose explanation -> iterator-mechanics prose+trace -> classification prose -> from-scratch code+diagram -> mine/real comparison -> exercise -> measured-cost code -> IQueryable prose+two code blocks -> two more varied exercises (find-the-bug, extend-the-code) -> sources. No wall-of-text stretch exceeds about 6-7 sentences before code or a figure breaks it up. This falls short of a 10 only because the depth and illustration are already close to exhaustive for the topic and no meaningfully better presentation choice was found; it is not held back by any concrete defect.
